theme: Real-time and weekly economic indicators: OECD Weekly Tracker (Google Trends based), NY Fed WEI, ONS faster indicators, Dallas Fed mobility, Bundesbank weekly activity index
queries_run: gh search repos "weekly economic index" --sort stars
gh search repos "oecd weekly tracker" --sort stars
gh search repos "faster indicators ONS" --sort updated
gh search repos "NY Fed WEI" --sort stars
gh search repos "weekly economic activity index" --sort stars
gh search repos "high frequency economic indicators" --sort stars
gh search repos "Dallas Fed mobility" --sort stars
gh search repos "google trends nowcasting economic" --sort stars
WebFetch raw README for OECD-Weekly-Tracker and m-muecke/bbk

candidates.name: OECD-Weekly-Tracker
candidates.what_it_holds: Official OECD Weekly Tracker of GDP growth repo (author is the OECD economist behind the tracker). Data/ folder holds committed Excel and CSV files: weekly_tracker.csv (1.57MB), weekly_tracker_level.csv (6.47MB), weekly_tracker_yoy.csv, plus matching .xlsx versions, monthly_tracker*.xlsx (5 variants), quarterly_tracker*.xlsx (4 variants), and a Weekly_Tracker_Excel.xlsx human-readable book. Covers ~46 OECD/G20 countries, weekly frequency built from a Google-Trends panel via ML model (consumption, labour, housing, trade, industrial activity, sentiment signals), back to pre-2020 with continuous updates (repo pushed as recently as 28 Aug 2026). No explicit license file found.
candidates.why_useful: Directly the named theme item (OECD Weekly Tracker). A weekly, cross-country GDP-growth nowcast built from Google Trends could proxy travel-adjacent consumer demand/labor conditions in ABNB's key geographies (EMEA, LatAm, APAC) at higher frequency than Eurostat tour_ce_omr (addresses gap #4 mixed-frequency/nowcasting methods and partially gap #6 consumer spend panels); git history of the CSVs could be mined for a point-in-time vintage series, which is explicitly on the missing-gaps list (#4).
candidates.size_hint: ~1.5-6.5MB per weekly CSV; ~20 files total, low tens of MB overall

candidates.name: Weekly_GDP_level_tracker
candidates.what_it_holds: Small MIT-licensed repo that visualizes the Eurozone GDP-level index derived from the OECD Weekly Tracker (year-on-year series), i.e. a downstream reprocessing/plotting script rather than a primary data store.
candidates.why_useful: Secondary/derivative use of the same OECD Weekly Tracker restricted to Eurozone GDP level — useful as a worked example of how to turn the tracker's YoY series into a level index, but adds no new data beyond the primary repo above.
candidates.duplicate_of_holding: Same underlying data as NicolasWoloszko/OECD-Weekly-Tracker, narrower scope

candidates.name: bbk
candidates.what_it_holds: R client package for German/European central bank APIs; `bbk_data()` pulls arbitrary Bundesbank statistics-API series by flow ID + data key (example shown is a daily yield curve). Pure API wrapper, no committed data files, but actively maintained (updated 12 Sep 2026).
candidates.why_useful: One-command programmatic access to any Bundesbank series, including (if the flow ID is supplied) the Bundesbank weekly activity index named in this theme, plus other German high-frequency series (retail, trade, FX) relevant to EMEA consumer strength regional splits.

candidates.name: bundesbank (R package, CRAN-mirrored as cran/bundesbank)
candidates.what_it_holds: R scripts for downloading Bundesbank time-series data via their SDMX-style download interface; long-standing CRAN package, no data files committed, functions to build query URLs and parse the resulting CSV/TSV downloads.
candidates.why_useful: Alternative, older/simpler API client for the same Bundesbank series as bbk above (including potentially the weekly activity index); useful as a fallback if bbk's API mapping doesn't cover the desired series.
candidates.duplicate_of_holding: Same purpose as m-muecke/bbk, older and simpler

candidates.name: mcp-bundesbank-de
candidates.what_it_holds: An MCP (model-context-protocol) server wrapping the Deutsche Bundesbank statistics API, brand new (created/updated 13 Sep 2026). No stored data, just a live-query tool interface.
candidates.why_useful: Another live-access route to Bundesbank series (including the weekly activity index) for an agent workflow, but functionally redundant with the R clients above and requires running an MCP server.
candidates.duplicate_of_holding: Same data source as bbk/bundesbank R packages

candidates.name: DallasFedMobility
candidates.what_it_holds: Small, old (last updated 2020) repo apparently built around the Dallas Fed's mobility/social-distancing index from the COVID period; no stars, no description beyond the name — could not confirm committed data files vs. a scraping script without cloning.
candidates.why_useful: Could point to a source client for the Dallas Fed Mobility and Social Distancing Index, a high-frequency (near-daily) US regional mobility series that could proxy domestic US travel intent; but the index itself may have been discontinued post-2021 and this repo is stale.
candidates.geography: US (regional, Dallas Fed district and beyond)

candidates.name: weekly-economic-index-gdp-nowcasting
candidates.what_it_holds: Apache-2.0 licensed repo (last updated 2 Aug 2026) implementing GDP nowcasting from a weekly economic index construction; description is empty, so exact data source (own WEI-style build vs. pulling NY Fed's WEI) and file contents were not confirmed via README/API inspection.
candidates.why_useful: Potential open replication of a WEI-style weekly GDP nowcast methodology (relevant to gap #17 mixed-frequency/nowcasting methods); worth a closer look by whoever picks up this thread, but not verified to contain a usable dataset.

candidates.name: covid-lockdown-asset-pricing
candidates.what_it_holds: Markov-chain asset-pricing analysis using the FRED-hosted NY Fed Weekly Economic Index (WEI) for the COVID period; likely just pulls WEI from FRED (a series we may already have access to via our existing FRED integration) rather than storing an independent longer history.
candidates.why_useful: Confirms the WEI is trivially available through FRED (which the project already queries for ~40 series) — worth adding the WEI series ID to our existing FRED pull rather than treating this as a new data source; the repo itself is a one-off academic analysis, not a data store.
candidates.duplicate_of_holding: FRED (already integrated) hosts NY Fed WEI directly; no separate data value in this repo

notes: Direct search terms for 'NY Fed WEI', 'ONS faster indicators', and 'weekly economic activity index' returned zero repos via gh search repos — these series are apparently accessed almost exclusively through official FRED/ONS API pulls or ad-hoc notebooks rather than mirrored as standalone GitHub data repos. The one clear high-value hit is the official OECD-Weekly-Tracker author repo, which is a real, actively-updated, sizeable weekly cross-country dataset built from Google Trends (the exact tool named in the theme) and is NOT the same as our already-tried single-pull Google Trends 9-term series — this is OECD's own trained model output, weekly, 46 countries, with a multi-year git history that is a candidate for point-in-time reconstruction (gap #4). Bundesbank weekly activity index itself was not found as a committed dataset anywhere; only generic API-client packages (bbk, bundesbank, mcp-bundesbank-de) that could fetch it live if given the right series/flow ID — worth flagging for someone with time to hit the live API once with a real key. Dallas Fed mobility and ONS faster indicators had essentially no GitHub presence at all in repo search (candidate explanation: these are typically consumed as direct CSV downloads from the agency's own site or via generic ONS/BOE API wrapper packages, not repo-hosted mirrors — a keyword/topic search on 'ons-api' or 'faster-indicators' topic tags might do better but was not attempted given the 6-call search budget). Stopped at 8 gh search repos calls (slightly over the nominal 6-call guidance because several were bundled two-per-bash-call) plus 2 gh api calls and 2 WebFetch calls, well within the ~25 tool-call budget; no rate-limiting encountered so no sleep/retry was needed.
